The spatial analysis skills in this lab — building `sf` objects from multiple sources, transforming coordinate reference systems, computing distances to boundaries, and identifying features within threshold zones — are the same operations you will apply to watersheds, river networks, gauge networks, and dam inventories throughout this course.

Before those datasets become available, we need the techniques to be automatic. This lab builds them on a familiar, nationally relevant dataset: US cities. Every operation you perform here — `st_union`, `st_combine`, `st_cast`, `st_distance`, `st_transform`, `gghighlight` — transfers directly to vector water resources data.

The payoff is Q4: a real-world application of these spatial skills to a live federal policy question that affects more Americans than most people realize. When you finish, you will have the tools to apply the same analysis to any spatial threshold problem.

This lab connects directly to recent policy discussions about border enforcement and the so-called "100-mile" border zone — for example, shifts in migration policy after the end of the pandemic-era Title 42 expulsions in 2023 have renewed attention on how proximity to the border affects enforcement, resource allocation, and civil liberties (see recent coverage: https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-ceases-using-title-42-pandemic-order-control-migration-2023-05-11/).

More recent operational discussions involving ICE and border enforcement through 2025–2026 have emphasized how interior and border-zone enforcement strategies depend on distance-to-border metrics; readers can consult summaries on civil-liberties implications (ACLU) or policy analyses that discuss the "100-mile" enforcement footprint for background: https://www.aclu.org/know-your-rights/border-zone, https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/blog/border-patrol-charlotte-atlanta-100-mile-zone/.

# Background

In this lab four main spatial skills are covered:

1. **Building** `sf` objects from R packages and CSV files — Q1
2. **Manipulating** geometries and coordinate systems — Q2
3. **Calculating** distances using geometry type selection — Q2
4. **Visualizing** spatial patterns with `ggplot2`, `gghighlight`, and `ggrepel` — Q3 & Q4

::: callout-tip
## Why these skills matter for water resources
Computing distance from a point to a boundary is one of the most common operations in spatial hydrology: distance from a gauge to a watershed outlet, distance from a city to the nearest floodplain, distance from a well to the nearest stream. The mechanics are identical regardless of what the features represent — master them here and they transfer everywhere.
:::

# **Question 1**: Build Your Spatial Dataset {#q1}

For this lab we need three datasets:

1. CONUS state boundaries (1.1)
2. North American country boundaries — US, Mexico, Canada (1.2)
3. All US cities (1.3)

## 1.1 Define a Projection

Distance calculations require a projected coordinate system that minimizes distance distortion at the scale of CONUS. We will use the **North America Equidistant Conic**:

```{r}
#| code-fold: false
eqdc <- '+proj=eqdc +lat_0=40 +lon_0=-96 +lat_1=20 +lat_2=60 +x_0=0 +y_0=0 +datum=NAD83 +units=m +no_defs'
```

This PROJ string defines:

| Parameter | Value | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `+proj=eqdc` | — | Equidistant Conic projection |
| `+lat_0=40` | 40°N | Latitude of projection center |
| `+lon_0=-96` | 96°W | Central meridian |
| `+lat_1=20`, `+lat_2=60` | 20°N, 60°N | Standard parallels |
| `+datum=NAD83` | — | North American Datum 1983 |
| `+units=m` | — | Output in meters |

Distortion is minimized between the two standard parallels — 20°N and 60°N encompasses all of CONUS, making this projection well-suited for national-scale distance analysis.

## 1.2 CONUS State Boundaries

Use `tigris::states()` to get US state boundaries, filter to CONUS, and transform to the equidistant projection.

::: callout-tip
`tigris` is the modern, CRAN-stable replacement for `USAboundaries`. It pulls boundaries directly from the US Census Bureau TIGER/Line files. Load the data with `states(cb = TRUE, progress_bar = FALSE)`. Filter the state codes (`STUSPS` column) to exclude Alaska, Hawaii, and US territories, then apply `st_transform(eqdc)` to reproject.
:::

```{r}
States <- tigris::states(cb = TRUE, progress_bar = FALSE) |>
  filter(STUSPS %in% state.abb, !STUSPS %in% c("AK", "HI")) |>
  st_transform(eqdc)
```

## 1.3 North American Country Boundaries

Use `rnaturalearth::ne_countries()` to get country boundaries for the United States, Canada, and Mexico.

::: callout-tip
`ne_countries()` returns an `sf` object directly when you specify `returnclass = "sf"`. Filter on the `admin` column to keep only the three countries you need, then transform to `eqdc`. See `?rnaturalearth::ne_countries` for available scales and parameters.
:::

```{r}
Countries <- rnaturalearth::ne_countries(scale = "medium", returnclass = "sf") |>
  filter(admin %in% c("United States of America", "Canada", "Mexico")) |>
  st_transform(eqdc)
```

## 1.4 US City Locations

Go to [simplemaps.com/data/us-cities](https://simplemaps.com/data/us-cities) and download the free basic dataset into your `data/` directory.

Read it in with `readr::read_csv()` and explore it — understand what columns are available before proceeding.

The raw data is tabular — coordinates are stored as numeric columns, not geometry. Convert it to a spatial object using `st_as_sf()`, specifying which columns hold X and Y coordinates and what CRS they use. Raw lat/lon from a CSV is almost always WGS84 (EPSG:4326).

::: callout-tip
After creating the `sf` object, you'll need to remove rows that fall outside CONUS. The `st_union(states)` geometry provides a boundary to filter against. See `?sf::st_filter` for how to select geometries that intersect or fall within a bounding polygon.
:::

```{r}
Cities <- readr::read_csv("C:/Users/jocel/OneDrive/Desktop/ESS523C/csu-523c/simplemaps_uscities_basicv1.93/uscities.csv") |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lng", "lat"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(eqdc) |>
  st_filter(st_union(States), .predicate = st_intersects)
```

::: callout-important
## Verify all three datasets before proceeding

Run these checks before moving to Q2 — a CRS mismatch here will silently corrupt every distance calculation downstream.

```{r}
# All three must return the same CRS
st_crs(States) == st_crs(Countries)
st_crs(States) == st_crs(Cities)

# Row counts should be reasonable
nrow(States)    # should be 48
nrow(Cities)    # should be ~28,000
```
:::

# **Question 2**: Distance Calculations {#q2}

Here we calculate the distance from each US city to four boundaries:

1. The US national border (coastline + land borders, resolved)
2. The nearest state border (internal boundaries preserved)
3. The Mexican border
4. The Canadian border

In all cases, since we want distance to a **border** (a line), we must cast our polygon geometries to `MULTILINESTRING` before computing distances. The choice of `st_union` vs. `st_combine` determines whether interior boundaries are dissolved or preserved — a distinction that matters for questions 2.1 and 2.2.

::: callout-tip
## The geometry type determines the answer

- `POLYGON` / `MULTIPOLYGON` → distance to the interior is **0** (you're inside the area)
- `MULTILINESTRING` → distance to the **boundary line** — what we actually want

```r
# Wrong: distance to a polygon
st_distance(city_point, state_polygon)   # returns 0 if city is inside

# Right: distance to the border
st_distance(city_point, state_polygon |> st_cast("MULTILINESTRING"))
```
:::

## 2.1 Distance to US National Border (km)

The national border is the **resolved** outer boundary of all states — internal state lines dissolved, only the coastline and land borders remain.

::: callout-tip
Use `st_union()` to merge all state polygons into a single boundary (dissolving internal borders), then cast to `MULTILINESTRING` so distances are measured to the **border line** rather than interior. Compute distance using `st_distance()` and convert the result to kilometers using `set_units()` from the `units` package — this ensures clean numeric output and correct unit handling downstream.
:::

Store the result as a new column `dist_to_border` in your cities data frame. Produce a **flextable** of the 5 cities farthest from the national border — include city name, state, and distance.

```{r}
States_Boundary <- States |>
  st_union() |>
  st_cast("MULTILINESTRING")

Cities <- Cities |>
  mutate(dist_to_border = st_distance(geometry, States_Boundary),
    dist_to_border = set_units(dist_to_border, "km"))

Cities |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(city, state_name, dist_to_border) |>
  arrange(desc(dist_to_border)) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  flextable() |>
  set_header_labels(city = "City", state_name = "State", dist_to_border = "Distance to Border") |>
  set_caption("Table 1. Listed are the 5 cities that are furthest from a national border in North America.") |>
  autofit()
```

## 2.2 Distance to Nearest State Border (km)

The nearest state border uses **preserved** internal boundaries — we want every state line, not just the outer edge. Use `st_combine()` which keeps all boundaries, then cast to `MULTILINESTRING`.

Store as `dist_to_state`. Produce a flextable of the 5 cities farthest from any state border.

::: callout-tip
Think carefully about why the answers for 2.1 and 2.2 differ. The city farthest from the national border might be close to a state line. The city farthest from any state line must be far from all internal AND external borders.
:::

```{r}
States_Boundary2 <- States |>
  st_combine() |>
  st_cast("MULTILINESTRING")

Cities <- Cities |>
  mutate(dist_to_state = st_distance(geometry, States_Boundary2),
    dist_to_state = set_units(dist_to_state, "km"))

Cities |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(city, state_name, dist_to_state) |>
  arrange(desc(dist_to_state)) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  flextable() |>
  set_header_labels(city = "City", state_name = "State", dist_to_state = "Distance to State Border") |>
  set_caption("Table 2. Listed are the 5 cities that are furhtest from a U.S. state border")|>
  autofit()
```

## 2.3 Distance to Mexico (km)

Isolate Mexico from your countries object. Cast to `MULTILINESTRING`. Compute distance from each city to the Mexican border. Store as `dist_to_mexico`. Produce a flextable of the 5 cities farthest from Mexico.

```{r}
Mexico_Boundary <- Countries |>
  filter(admin == "Mexico") |>
  st_cast("MULTILINESTRING")

Cities <- Cities |>
  mutate(dist_to_mexico = st_distance(geometry, Mexico_Boundary),
    dist_to_mexico = set_units(dist_to_mexico, "km"))

Cities |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(city, state_name, dist_to_mexico) |>
  arrange(desc(dist_to_mexico)) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  flextable() |>
  set_header_labels(city = "City", state_name = "State", dist_to_mexico = "Distance to Mexico") |>
  set_caption("Table 3. Listed are the 5 cities that are furthest from The Mexican border.") |>
  autofit()
```

## 2.4 Distance to Canada (km)

Same approach as 2.3, for Canada. Store as `dist_to_canada`. Produce a flextable of the 5 cities farthest from Canada.

```{r}
Canada_Boundary <- Countries |>
  filter(admin == "Canada") |>
  st_cast("MULTILINESTRING")

Cities <- Cities |>
  mutate(dist_to_canada = st_distance(geometry, Canada_Boundary ),
    dist_to_canada = set_units(dist_to_canada, "km"))

Cities |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(city, state_name, dist_to_canada) |>
  arrange(desc(dist_to_canada)) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  flextable() |>
  set_header_labels(city = "City", state_name = "State", dist_to_canada = "Distance to Canada") |>
  set_caption("Table 4. Listed are the 5 cities that are furthest from the Canadian border.") |>
  autofit()
```

# **Question 3**: Mapping Distance Patterns {#q3}

Now visualize the distance data you computed. You will use `ggplot2` for all maps, `ggrepel::geom_label_repel()` for non-overlapping city labels, and `gghighlight` to emphasize subsets.

## 3.1 Reference Map

Create a base reference map showing:

- North America (US, Canada, Mexico) as filled grey polygons
- CONUS state boundaries as dashed lines
- The 10 largest US cities by population as labeled points

::: callout-tip
Use `geom_sf()` for spatial layers. For labels that don't overlap:

```r
ggrepel::geom_label_repel(
  data = big_cities,
  aes(geometry = geometry, label = city),
  stat = "sf_coordinates",
  size = 3
)
```

`stat = "sf_coordinates"` extracts point coordinates from the geometry for label placement — required when using `ggrepel` with `sf` objects.
:::

```{r}
Big_Cities <- Cities |>
  slice_max(population, n = 10)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = Countries, fill = "grey") +
  geom_sf(data = States, fill = NA,linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_sf(data = Big_Cities) +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(
    data = Big_Cities,
    aes(geometry = geometry, label = city),
    stat = "sf_coordinates",
    size = 3) +
  labs(caption = "Figure 1. 10 cities with the largest U.S. populations.") +
  theme_linedraw()
```

## 3.2 Distance to National Border

Color all US cities by their distance to the national border using a continuous color scale. Highlight and label the 5 cities farthest from the border.

Your map should:
- Use `scale_color_viridis_c()` for the distance gradient
- Show the CONUS outline
- Label the 5 farthest cities with `ggrepel`

```{r}
Furthest5_Cities <- Cities |>
  slice_max(dist_to_border, n = 5)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = Cities, aes(color = drop_units(dist_to_border))) +
  geom_sf(data = States, fill = NA, color = "grey70", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = Furthest5_Cities, color = "black") +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(
    data = Furthest5_Cities,
    aes(geometry = geometry, label = city),
    stat = "sf_coordinates",
    size = 3) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Distance to National Border (km)") +
  labs(caption = "Figure 2. 5 furthest cities from an international border, colored by border distance.") +
  theme_linedraw()
```

In 2–3 sentences: (1) where are the cities farthest from the national border? (2) Does the geographic pattern make sense given the shape of CONUS? (3) Name one water resources application where distance to a national border would be a meaningful variable.

> The five cities farthest from the national border are all located in Kansas. This pattern makes sense given the shape of CONUS, as cities in the geographic center of the country are farthest from any coastline or international boundary, and distances decrease toward the edge. One water resources application where this matters is interstate/international water delivery; if headwaters are far from a border, meeting downstream delivery obligations could be more challenging as resources deminish overtime (Eturm et al. 2017).

Sturm et al. (2017). Water and Life from Snow: A Trillion Dollar Science Question. Water 
Resources Research 53, 3534-3544. https://doi.org/10.1002/2017WR020840. 


## 3.3 Distance to Nearest State Border

Color all cities by distance to the nearest state border. Highlight and label the 5 cities farthest from any state line.

```{r}
Furthest5_States <- Cities |>
  arrange(desc(dist_to_state)) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = Cities, aes(color = drop_units(dist_to_state))) +
  geom_sf(data = States, fill = NA, color = "black", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_sf(data = Furthest5_States) +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(
    data = Furthest5_States,
    aes(geometry = geometry, label = city),
    stat = "sf_coordinates",
    size = 3) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Distance to State Border (km)") +
  labs(caption = "Figure 3. 5 U.S. states that are furthest from a state border.") +
  theme_linedraw()
```

In 2–3 sentences: (1) how does the pattern differ from 3.2? (2) Which states appear to have the largest interior areas — do any water resources features (large river basins, aquifer extents) correlate with the states where cities can be far from borders? (3) What would a hydrologist use this distance for?

> The pattern in 3.3 differs from 3.2 because it reflects distance to state boundaries rather than the national border, resulting in multiple interior areas rather then a single central region. States like Texas and Montana show large interior areas, which aligns with their extensive river basins and aquifer systems like the Edwards and Ogallala aquifers in Texas and the mountainous watershed basins in Montana (Montana n.d.; Texas n.d.). A hydrologist could use this distance to understand how far water travels within a state before crossing certain boundaries, this is important for managing water allocation, groundwater recharge, and interstate/international water agreements.

- Texas Water Development Board. (n.d.). Groundwater. https://www.twdb.texas.gov/groundwater/index.asp.

- Montana Department of Natural Resources and Conservation. (n.d.). State Water Plan & Regional Basin Plans. https://dnrc.mt.gov/Water-Resources/Water-Planning-Implementation-and-Communications/State-Water-Plan-Regional-Basin-Plans/.

## 3.4 Equidistance Zone: Mexico and Canada

Identify cities that are **approximately equidistant** from the Mexican and Canadian borders — within ±100 km of equal distance from both.

::: callout-tip
Create a variable for the absolute difference between the two distances, then use `gghighlight()` to emphasize cities where that difference is less than 100 km. Label the 5 most populous cities in this zone with `ggrepel`.
:::

```{r}
Cities <- Cities |>
  mutate(Equidistant = abs(dist_to_mexico - dist_to_canada),
    Equidistant_km = drop_units(Equidistant),
    Equidistant_Zone = Equidistant_km <= 100)

Equidistant_Cities <- Cities |>
  filter(Equidistant_Zone) |>
  arrange(desc(population)) |>
  slice_head(n = 5)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = Cities) +
  geom_sf(data = States) +
  geom_sf(data = Cities |> filter(Equidistant_Zone),
    aes(color = Equidistant_km)) +
  geom_sf(data = Equidistant_Cities) +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(data = Equidistant_Cities,
    aes(geometry = geometry, label = city), stat = "sf_coordinates") +
  gghighlight::gghighlight(n = 5, unhighlighted_params = list(alpha = 0.1)) +
  labs(caption = "Figure 4. 5 U.S. states equidistant from the Canadian and Mexican borders.") +
  scale_color_viridis_c(name = "Equidistance (Mexico-Canada; km)")

## This code was not working for me so I plugged it into ChatGBT version 5.3 and it added the line "Equidistant_km = drop_units(Equidistant)" due to Error in "`ggplot_add()`: ! All calculations failed! Please provide a valid predicate. Run `rlang::last_trace()` to see where the error occurred."

## - OpenAI. (2026). ChatGPT (GPT-5.3) ["Why is my code not running (including code and error message)]. https://chat.openai.com/.
```

In 2–3 sentences: (1) describe where the equidistant zone runs geographically, (2) does it surprise you that this band cuts through the interior of the country where it does? (3) What does this zone imply about the relative influence of Canadian vs. Mexican climate systems on cities in this corridor?

> The equidistant zone runs diagonally from the southeastern United States (around Georgia), to Kansas) and towards California. It is not surprising that the band cuts through the interior in this way since the midpoint it is in the middle of the country, but in the east the influence of the Gulf of Mexico is unseen creating confusion upon first glance. This zone suggests that cities along it will experience equal influence from climate systems coming from both Canadian and Mexican.

# **Question 4**: Real-World Application — The 100-Mile Border Zone {#q4}

## Background

Federal regulations give U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) authority to operate within **100 miles of any US "external boundary"** — including both land borders and coastlines. Within this zone, CBP agents can conduct stops and searches without a warrant or reasonable suspicion. Federal courts have repeatedly upheld this authority.

The American Civil Liberties Union has documented and challenged this policy. Their analysis is [here](https://www.aclu.org/other/constitution-100-mile-border-zone).

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
knitr::include_graphics('C:/Users/jocel/OneDrive/Desktop/ESS523C/03-aclu.jpg')
```

100 miles ≈ **160 kilometers**. Your distance calculations are already in kilometers.

## 4.1 Quantify the Zone

Using your `dist_to_border` column, calculate:

- How many cities fall within the 100-mile zone?
- What is the total population living in cities within the zone?
- What percentage of the total US city population does this represent?
- Does your result match the ACLU's published estimate?

Present your findings as a formatted **flextable**.

::: callout-tip
Filter to cities within 160 km, drop geometry if needed, then summarize: count rows (`n()`), sum population, and compute the percentage relative to total city population. You will need to reference total city population across the *entire dataset*, not just filtered rows — plan your calculation carefully.
:::

```{r}
Population_Cities <- Cities |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarize(total = sum(population, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  pull(total)

Cities |>
  filter(dist_to_border <= set_units(160,"km")) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarize(n_cities = n(), Zone_Population = sum(population, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(Percent_Population = 100 * Zone_Population / Population_Cities) |>
  flextable()|>
  set_header_labels(n_cities = "# of Cities", Zone_Population = "Zone Population", Percent_Population = "% Population") |>
  set_caption("Table 5. The percent population was found to be ~65%, which matches the ACLU image.") |>
  autofit()
```

In 2–3 sentences: (1) report the percentage and compare it to the ACLU's estimate, (2) explain why the result might be higher than many people expect given the geography of the US, (3) name one scenario where a water resources professional might need to navigate federal jurisdictional boundaries in a similar way — where a regulatory zone defined by distance from a physical boundary changes what analysis or permitting is required.

>  The percentage calculated was about 65% of U.S. cities falling within the 100-mile border zone, which is consistent with the ACLU’s estimate of 2/3 of the population. This may seem higher than expected given the large interior areas of the United States, but clearly most of the population is concentrated near coasts and borders. A similar situation in water resources occurs when resource zones are defined by distance from features like rivers, causing potential for water allocation rules to change depending on how close you are to those resource boundaries.

## 4.2 Map the Zone

Create a map highlighting all cities within the 100-mile zone using `gghighlight`.

- Color cities by distance to the border using a gradient from `"orange"` to `"darkred"`
- Label the **10 most populous** cities in the zone

```{r}
Cities <- Cities |>
  mutate(Border_Zone = drop_units(dist_to_border) <= 160)

Cities_10Populous <- Cities |>
  filter(Border_Zone) |>
  arrange(desc(population)) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = Cities, color = "grey") +
  geom_sf(data = Cities |> filter(Border_Zone),
    aes(color = drop_units(dist_to_border))) +
  geom_sf(data = States, fill = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = Cities_10Populous) +
  ggrepel::geom_label_repel(data = Cities_10Populous,
    aes(geometry = geometry, label = city),
    stat = "sf_coordinates",
    size = 3) +
  labs(caption = "Figure 5. 10 most populous U.S. cities with the border zone (100-miles) highlighted.") +
  scale_color_gradient(low = "orange", high = "darkred", name = "Distance to Border (km)")
```

In 2–3 sentences: (1) how many states have at least one city in the zone? (2) Are there states where the most populous city is NOT in the zone — what does that tell you about that state's geography? (3) How might the jurisdictional boundary created by this rule create challenges for environmental monitoring programs that cross state or national boundaries?

> There are 25 states that have at least one city within the border zone. There are 14 states where the most populous city is not in this zone, suggesting that those states are either more centrally located or that their main developement occured away from border zones This type of jurisdictional boundary can create challenges for environmental monitoring programs, as conditions and regulations may differ across borders, requiring coordination of interstate/international management of resources.

# **Question 5**: Interactive Leaflet Exercise — Build an interactive map

This hands-on exercise ties the distance calculations and mapping skills from Q1–Q4 into a single interactive web map. The goal is a compact, well-documented Leaflet map with layer controls, informative popups, and two toggleable thematic layers: (A) the ±100 km equidistance band (Mexico vs Canada) and (B) the 100-mile (≈160 km) national-border zone.

Learning objectives:

- Practice turning `sf` results into interactive HTML widgets with `leaflet`.
- Build informative popups that show computed distances and metadata.
- Implement layer groups and a legend so users can toggle overlays.
- Consider performance and projection issues when publishing web maps.

## Deliverables

Create an interactive `leaflet` map that includes:

- **Base layers**: CONUS state boundaries and at least one provider tile basemap (e.g., CartoDB, OpenStreetMap)
- **Data layers** (toggleable via `addLayersControl`):
  - All cities colored by distance to the national border (use a color palette like `colorNumeric("viridis")`; see `?leaflet::colorNumeric`)
  - Cities in the equidistance zone (±100 km Mexico/Canada difference) highlighted separately
  - Cities in the 100-mile border zone highlighted separately
- **Popups**: When you click a city marker, display relevant information: city name, state, population, and distances to borders
- **Legend**: Show what the color scale represents

::: callout-tip
Key `leaflet` functions:
- `leaflet()` to initialize
- `addProviderTiles()` for basemaps
- `addCircleMarkers()` or `addMarkers()` for point data
- `addPolygons()` for state boundaries
- `addLegend()` for a color scale legend
- `addLayersControl()` to make layers toggleable

See `?leaflet` and the [Leaflet for R documentation](https://rstudio.github.io/leaflet/) for syntax and options. Remember that `leaflet` works with WGS84 coordinates (EPSG:4326), so you may need to transform your data before plotting.
:::

```{r}
library(leaflet)

Cities_Leaf <- Cities |>
  st_transform(4326) |>
  mutate(dist_to_border_km = drop_units(set_units(dist_to_border, "km")),
    dist_to_mexico_km = drop_units(set_units(dist_to_mexico, "km")),
    dist_to_canada_km = drop_units(set_units(dist_to_canada, "km")),
    mexico_canada_diff_km = abs(dist_to_mexico_km - dist_to_canada_km))

States_Leaf <- st_transform(States, 4326)

Color_Scheme <- leaflet::colorNumeric("viridis", domain = Cities_Leaf$dist_to_border_km)

Popup <- paste0("Population: ", Cities_Leaf$population, "<br/>",
  "Distance to National Border: ", round(Cities_Leaf$dist_to_border_km, 1), " km<br/>",
  "Distance to Mexico: ", round(Cities_Leaf$dist_to_mexico_km, 1), " km<br/>",
  "Distance to Canada: ", round(Cities_Leaf$dist_to_canada_km, 1), " km<br/>",
  "Mexico-Canada Difference: ", round(Cities_Leaf$mexico_canada_diff_km, 1), " km")

leaflet() |>
  leaflet::addProviderTiles(leaflet::providers$CartoDB.Positron, group = "Light") |>
  leaflet::addProviderTiles(leaflet::providers$Esri.WorldImagery, group = "Satellite") |>
  leaflet::addPolygons(data = States_Leaf, group = "States") |>
  leaflet::addCircleMarkers(data = Cities_Leaf, color = ~Color_Scheme(dist_to_border_km), radius = 2,
    stroke = FALSE, popup = Popup,
    group = "Distance to National Border") |>
  leaflet::addCircleMarkers(data = Cities_Leaf |> filter(Equidistant_Zone),
    color = "steelblue", radius = 5, stroke = TRUE,
    popup = Popup[Cities_Leaf$Equidistant_Zone],
    group = "Equidistance Zone (+/- 100 km)") |>
  leaflet::addCircleMarkers(data = Cities_Leaf |> filter(Border_Zone),
    color = "maroon", radius = 5,stroke = TRUE, popup = Popup[Cities_Leaf$Border_Zone],
    group = "Border Zone (100 miles)") |>
  leaflet::addLegend(pal = Color_Scheme, values = Cities_Leaf$dist_to_border_km,
    title = "Distance to National Border (km)") |>
  leaflet::addLayersControl(
    baseGroups = c("Light", "Satellite"),
    overlayGroups = c("States", "Distance to National Border", "Equidistance Zone (+/- 100 km)",
      "Border Zone (100 miles)"))
```

**Methods note**: In 2–3 sentences, describe the CRS transformation needed to convert from `eqdc` to `leaflet`-compatible coordinates, and any design choices you made to keep the map responsive (e.g., filtering, clustering, or simplifying geometries).

> The data originally were projected in the equidistant coordinate system (eqdc), I then transformed the data to WGS84 (EPSG:4326) using st_transform() for compatibility with leaflet. To keep the map responsive, I filtered and colored cities  within the equidistant zone between Canada and Mexico, the border zone, and total distance to the international borders. This reduced clutter and while maintaining a clear and interactive map.

# Summary

In this lab you:

- **Built** spatial datasets from three different sources: a CRAN package (`tigris`), a data package (`rnaturalearth`), and a downloaded CSV
- **Transformed** coordinate reference systems and selected a projection appropriate for national-scale distance analysis
- **Manipulated** geometry types — understanding when to use `st_union` vs. `st_combine`, and why casting to `MULTILINESTRING` is required before computing distances to borders
- **Computed** four sets of distances using `st_distance()` and stored them as labeled unit vectors
- **Visualized** spatial patterns with continuous color scales, `gghighlight`, and `ggrepel`
- **Built** an interactive web map using `leaflet` to present distance data to a general audience

Every one of these operations recurs in the labs ahead — applied to watersheds, river networks, elevation grids, and gauge networks. The mechanics are now yours.
